quote: (like the lottery winners who, six months later, aren’t nearly as happy as they expected to be)
content: The lottery-winner finding has reversed. The source is Brickman, Coates & Janoff-Bulman (1978): twenty-two Illinois lottery winners interviewed on average about a year after winning, not six months, who reported present happiness no higher than controls, with no measure of what they had “expected.” The study is cross-sectional, tiny, and its winner sample was recruited by mail with a low response rate. When the question was asked properly, with administrative data on thousands of Swedish lottery winners followed for up to twenty-two years, large wins produced sustained increases in life satisfaction and financial well-being that did not fade (Lindqvist, Östling & Cesarini (2020)). Book II’s annotations found the disability half of the Brickman study reversed by Lucas’s panel data; this is the other half. The hedonic-treadmill story the essay relies on for its central claim, that obtaining what you wanted stops it being wanted, was a small-sample artefact for the case it names.

quote: Born into a world of science, they did not become scientists. What makes them think that, in a world of magic, they would act any differently?
content: The question answers itself within the genre, which is why readers do not feel its force. In the standard portal fantasy the protagonist is chosen, gifted, or the last of a line; magic is distributed by birth or destiny, and the reader’s wish is to be selected, not to enrol. Where a fantasy world does treat magic as a discipline requiring years of study, that is the story’s subject (Le Guin’s A Wizard of Earthsea, Rothfuss’s The Name of the Wind, the entire magic-school subgenre), and those books are read in the same numbers, which suggests the readers are not averse to the studying. The essay’s premise, that a reader who did not become a scientist would not become a sorcerer, holds only if the two worlds distribute their powers the same way, and the fantasy is precisely that they do not. There is also a smaller empirical problem with “barring improbable demographics”: readership surveys of science fiction and fantasy have found technical and scientific occupations overrepresented since the 1970s, so the assumption that the readership is unscientific is itself an assumption. The essay’s point about the capacity for joy in the available may still be right. Its argument for it, from what the readers would do, assumes the readers’ fantasy is the one the essay would have.

quote: Matthew C., commenting on Less Wrong, seems very excited about an informally specified “theory” by Rupert Sheldrake which “explains” such non-explanation-demanding phenomena as protein folding and snowflake symmetry.
content: Sheldrake’s morphic resonance explains nothing, and the essay is right about that. But the two phenomena named were not, when the essay was written, “non-explanation-demanding.” Protein folding was the open problem the same author describes in Is Reality Ugly?, five essays earlier, as something “we still can’t predict”; Levinthal’s paradox (how a chain finds its native state in microseconds when a random search would take longer than the age of the universe) was an active research question until the funnel picture and, later, AlphaFold. Snowflake symmetry, the question of why the six arms of a single crystal match one another in detail while no two crystals match, was described by the field’s leading experimentalist in that year as depending on growth dynamics that “are not well understood” (Libbrecht (2005)), and remains partly open. Matthew C. was excited about a bad answer to two real questions. The essay, in dismissing the answer, dismisses the questions, and does so in a book whose refrain is that mystery is a fact about one’s state of mind, not about the phenomenon.
